recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what you divide by, and what you can say about sin x as x increases without bound.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Divide by x² and bound sin x
steps.margin_note: First mark. The examiner is looking for the words "sin x lies between −1 and 1". Dividing by x² alone is not the full method.
lines: Divide the numerator and the denominator by x² (x ≠ 0):

recall.must_convey: That both lines are divided by x², and that sin x always lies between −1 and 1.
accept: divide by x squared and use that sine x stays between minus one and one
sine x is bounded so sine x over x squared goes to zero
sine never goes outside minus one to one
sine x eppudu minus one and one madhya untundi
divide throughout by x squared first

steps.why: sin x has no limit as x increases without bound, so it cannot be handled on its own. It can be handled as a bounded quantity: it always lies between −1 and 1, while x² increases without bound.
common_mistakes: Writing lim(x → ∞) sin x = 0; sin x keeps oscillating between −1 and 1 and has no limit.
Cancelling x² against sin x as though sin x were a factor.
steps.memory_tip: A bounded quantity divided by one that increases without bound approaches 0.

steps.label: Take the limit
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Box 1. Both outer bounds −1/x² and 1/x² approach 0, so the quantity between them does as well.
lines: As x → ∞,  1/x² → 0, so by the Sandwich theorem (sin x)/x² → 0

recall.must_convey: That (sin x)/x² → 0 and 2/x² → 0, so the value is 1.
accept: both correction terms go to zero so the answer is one
sine x over x squared goes to zero by the sandwich theorem
rendu terms zero ayipothayi, answer one

steps.why: Both correction terms approach 0, so the quotient approaches 1/1. The sine term changes nothing because it is divided by a quantity that increases without bound.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as (1 − sin x)/1 with sin x still present.
Cancelling the x² terms first and reading (−sin x)/(−2), which gives no limit at all.
steps.memory_tip: Both lines are led by x², so the answer is 1; the sine only adds a correction that approaches 0.
